standard.title: First Nations visual arts
standard.description: explore examples of visual arts created by First Nations Australians
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have begun to explore arts across cultures and communities (AC9AVA2E01). They have some awareness that arts serve different purposes in different communities. They have not yet specifically explored First Nations Australian visual arts or the concept of Country/Place in art-making.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explore examples of visual arts created by First Nations Australians, identifying how these artworks communicate connection to Country/Place and cultural identity.

nodes.label: Country/Place in First Nations visual arts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify that many First Nations Australian artworks feature Country/Place as central — connecting where we are to who we are.
nodes.minimum_width: Look at one First Nations Australian artwork and identify one way it represents or communicates place.
nodes.typical_width: Explore artworks by First Nations Australian artists that feature places as central; discuss what the artworks communicate about why place is part of identity; engage with artists' own voices through culturally authoritative resources.
wider: Listen to First Nations Australian artists describe the importance of Country/Place to their art-making — using resources created or co-created by First Nations Australians
Explore artworks that represent First Nations Australians' interpretations of the night sky — discuss how different times of year and different perspectives shape the sky as subject matter
nodes.hinge_reason: The Country/Place concept is foundational to understanding First Nations Australian visual arts at this level — without it, students interpret these artworks through a generic 'landscape' lens that misses the cultural function.

response_modes.reason: The concept that place is part of identity is culturally unfamiliar for many students. Explicit discussion with prompts ('Why might where you are be part of who you are?') is needed before students can engage with the artworks meaningfully.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one way a First Nations Australian artwork represents or communicates place
Explains why place might be important to the artist or their community

nodes.label: Visual conventions in First Nations arts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can observe specific visual conventions (colours, symbols, patterns) used in First Nations Australian artworks and connect them to cultural meaning.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one visual convention (colour, symbol or pattern) in a First Nations Australian artwork and share one observation about why it might be used.
nodes.typical_width: Observe how visual conventions are used in a range of First Nations Australian artworks; discuss colours, symbols and patterns with guidance from culturally authoritative resources or community representatives; connect conventions to cultural meanings.
wider: Co-create symbols and designs to represent patterns visible in the night sky at different times of year — do this with First Nations Australians who have cultural authority
Explore First Nations Australian cultural expressions in community settings and at national events — identify how artists observe protocols and respect Elders or knowledge holders

response_modes.reason: Students need to engage with a range of First Nations Australian visual arts rather than a single example to develop genuine understanding — diverse artists, regions and forms prevent the misconception that all First Nations art looks the same.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The diversity of First Nations Australian visual arts across regions and cultural contexts is genuinely rich — students who engage with a range develop respect for this diversity rather than a homogenised view.
success_criteria: Identifies at least one visual convention in a First Nations Australian artwork
Shares one observation about what the convention might mean or communicate

nodes.label: First Nations arts in community and national life
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify where First Nations Australian cultural expressions appear in their lives and communities, and recognise that artists follow cultural protocols.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one place or occasion where First Nations Australian cultural expressions are present (in community, at national events, at school).
nodes.typical_width: Explore how First Nations Australian cultural expressions appear in community and national life; notice ways that artists observe protocols and respect Elders; connect these observations to the earlier understanding of arts as important for communities.
wider: Explore artworks connected to significant occasions (NAIDOC Week, Reconciliation Week, Sorry Day) — investigate how these artworks serve community and cultural purposes
Use Viewpoints questions to co-create an inquiry about a First Nations Australian artist and their practice — investigate what the work teaches about their community and Country

response_modes.reason: Students bring together their understanding of Country/Place, visual conventions and cultural community functions to see First Nations visual arts as a living, ongoing practice — not a historical artefact.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one place or occasion where First Nations Australian cultural expressions appear
Shows awareness that artists follow cultural protocols and that these are meaningful
